metadata.title: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Evaluating the Safety of New Drugs for Improving Glycemic Control Guidance for Industry
metadata.legal_basis: FDA Guidance Document (21 CFR 10.115). Guidance states FDA's current thinking and is not binding unless a statute or regulation requires it; the official text governs.

metadata_verification: Source-register metadata; dates and legal status require human verification.
limitations: English rule-based extraction; no GPT or paid API.

candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 40 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 41 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 42 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 43 not required. 44
candidates.context: This guidance is intended to serve as a focus for continued discussions among the Division of 36 Metabolism and Endocrinology Products, pharmaceutical sponsors, the academic community, 37 and the public. 4

candidates.statement: The withdrawn Diabetes Mellitus December 2008 guidance stated that sponsors should 49 demonstrate that new drugs intended to improve glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes 50 do not result in an unacceptable increase in CV risk. In response to the 2008 guidance, many 51 CVOTs have been completed. In reviewing those final reports, the Agency has found that 52 inclusion of meaningful numbers of patients with diabetes-associated complications and 53 comorbid conditions in clinical trials is feasible and valuable in assessing the safety profile of 54 new antidiabetic drugs, allowing valid assessment of CV risk. However, none of the CVOTs to 55 date have identified an increased risk of ischemic CV events. Some of the CVOTs have instead 56 demonstrated a reduced risk for CV events. 57
candidates.context: In light of these CVOT results, the Agency convened an advisory committee meeting on October 59 24–25, 2018, to discuss the recommendations in the Diabetes Mellitus December 2008 guidance. 60 Committee members were asked to consider the robustness of development program safety 61 databases before 2008, the new information learned since 2008, and whether the 62 recommendations in the Diabetes Mellitus December 2008 guidance were still appropriate. 63 Committee members stressed the need for sufficient safety data submitted before approval to 64 inform decision-making, the continued importance of CV safety data not limited to 65 atherosclerotic events, and the need to base postmarketing requirements on consideration of 66 signals of risk identified in the development program rather than a one-size-fits-all approach. 67

candidates.statement: Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus require chronic therapy, generally for many years. Given 79 the prevalence of diabetes, substantial patient exposure can be expected. Therefore, drugs 80 approved to improve glycemic control in these patients should have well-characterized safety 81 profiles based on shorter term studies, but some safety concerns may only be identified in longer 82 term studies. For these reasons, the safety database of a new antidiabetic drug for type 2 diabetes 83 mellitus should also include a substantial number of patients exposed to the drug for longer 84 periods to allow for a thorough assessment of the drug’s longer term safety profile. Therefore, 85 the safety database for a marketing application for a new drug for glycemic control should 86 include data from controlled clinical trials and controlled clinical trial extensions with the 87 following exposures: 88
candidates.context: A. Size of the Safety Database 77 1) At least 4,000 patient-years of exposure to the new drug in phase 3 clinical trials. (This 90 exposure includes all dosage strengths studied in the phase 3 clinical trials.) 91

candidates.statement: Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus often have comorbid conditions and/or diabetes-associated 99 complications (e.g., chronic kidney disease, CV disease). Therefore, it is important to evaluate 100 the safety of new drugs to improve glycemic control in the population of patients who will be 101 using the drugs, including a meaningful number of patients with underlying CV disease, chronic 102 kidney disease, and older patients. When a sponsor submits a marketing application for a new 103 drug for glycemic control, the safety database should include data from patients with relevant 104 age, comorbid conditions, and/or complications in the phase 3 trials as follows: 105
candidates.context: B. Patient Characteristics in the Development Program 97 1) At least 500 patients with stage 3/4 chronic kidney disease exposed to the new drug. 107

candidates.statement: Recognizing that a given patient could fall into more than one of these three categories, sponsors 115 should aim for at least 1,200 patients with at least one of these conditions. 116
candidates.context: 3) At least 600 patients older than 65 years of age exposed to the new drug. 113 C. Other Considerations 118

candidates.statement: Sponsors should also consider the following concerning the collection of safety data: 120
candidates.context: C. Other Considerations 118 • Adverse CV outcomes remain an important source of morbidity and mortality for patients 122 with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Therefore, sponsors should use rigorous methods for the 123 collection of adverse CV events and assess them by adjudication. 124

candidates.context: Sponsors should also consider the following concerning the collection of safety data: 120 • In some cases, the evaluation of a premarket safety concern may require that a drug 126 development program accrue a minimum number of relevant adverse events to exclude a 127 meaningful degree of risk. Adjudication of these adverse events may also be needed. 128 The Agency expects that situations where the collection of these additional safety data is 129 necessary will be identified and discussed before phase 3 trials are initiated. 130

candidates.statement: • Sponsors should include data safety monitoring boards or committees to provide 132 independent oversight of the safety findings from the clinical trials. 133
